opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think science is one of the clearest historical examples we have of a social technology that lets people converge on the truth even when individuals have strong incentives to believe or argue otherwise. If you look at the period before the scientific revolution, you had plenty of very smart people, but questions about the natural world were often settled by appeal to authority, to tradition, or to what was politically or religiously convenient. And people's reasoning was bent by all the usual things: status, tribal loyalty, wanting your own theory to be right.

What changed wasn't that scientists became saints who stopped having motivated reasoning. Individual scientists remain quite biased in favor of their own hypotheses, and there are famous cases of people clinging to theories long past when the evidence turned against them. Max Planck's quip that science advances one funeral at a time captures some of that. The key innovation was institutional: a set of norms and practices that made it possible for the truth to win out at the level of the community even when individuals were biased.

So you have things like the norm of reproducible experiments, where a claim isn't accepted just because a prestigious person made it, but because others can go and check it. You have publication and open sharing of methods and data, so errors can be found. You have a reward structure where you can gain status by overturning an established view if you actually have the evidence, which channels people's competitive and status-seeking motives toward finding flaws in others' work. And especially in the more mature sciences, you have quantitative prediction, where a theory makes precise forecasts that either come true or don't, and that's very hard to spin.

The result is that in areas where those conditions hold strongly, say physics or chemistry, you get remarkable consensus and reliability, and the consensus tends to track reality. You can trust the claim that a bridge design will hold, or that a drug has a certain chemical structure, even though you personally haven't checked it, because the system has strong error-correcting properties.

That's encouraging as a precedent, because it shows that a society's epistemic capacity isn't fixed by human psychology. With the right institutions and the right tools, you can get much better collective truth-tracking out of the same flawed individual reasoners. It also suggests where the gaps are. Science works much less well where you can't do clean experiments, where feedback is slow, or where questions are politically charged: large parts of social science, policy, forecasting long-run consequences. There, motivated reasoning still dominates to a much greater degree.

And that's part of why I'm interested in how AI could extend this. If you had AI systems that were trustworthy, that could do the equivalent of checking the work, running analyses, and giving well-calibrated assessments, and whose reliability could itself be verified through track records and testing, you might extend something like the scientific community's error correction into domains where we currently can't get it. Just as science let us establish trusted facts about chemistry that nobody seriously disputes regardless of their politics, you could hope for a world where more contested empirical questions get settled in a similar way. Of course that depends on getting the incentives and verification right, just as science did, rather than having AI that tells each faction what it wants to hear.

r001.rationale: The response discusses authority and individual bias, but does not say scholars reciprocally supported one another to sustain dogmatic authority.

r002.rationale: It says science works less well without clean experiments, but does not identify insulation from experimental feedback as what preserved scholarly dogmatism.

r003.rationale: The response does not express that science would eventually have emerged even if the historical Scientific Revolution had been prevented.

r004.rationale: It describes science’s reliability and practical trustworthiness, but does not explain that demonstrated practical value helped truth-tracking methods gain societal influence despite motivated opposition.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so I think the history of science is actually one of the most encouraging precedents we have, because the prior situation was really bad. For most of human history, people's beliefs about the natural world were dominated by things like religious authority, deference to ancient texts, whatever was socially convenient, whatever flattered the people in power. And individual humans today are not that different from individual humans then — we still have the same cognitive biases, the same tendency to believe what's comfortable or what our group believes.

What changed wasn't the people, it was the institutions and the norms. You got things like the expectation that claims should be backed by experiments that other people can replicate. You got the norm that you publish your methods so that others can check them. You got a reward structure where you can gain status by overturning an established result — so there's actually an incentive for somebody to go and find the flaw in the consensus, rather than everyone having an incentive to go along with it. Peer review, for all its problems, means that a claim gets scrutinised by people who are at least somewhat adversarial. And then there's the brute fact of contact with reality: if your theory of chemistry is wrong, your reactions don't work, your bridges fall down, and that feedback is hard to argue with.

And the result is that science has made enormous progress in domains where there's that kind of feedback, even though the individual scientists are just as motivated, just as ambitious, just as prone to fooling themselves as anyone else. Motivated reasoning didn't go away — scientists absolutely want their pet theories to be true — but the system was set up so that the collective output is a lot more accurate than any individual's reasoning would be.

Now, the places where it works least well are instructive too. In fields where experiments are expensive or impossible, or where the results have big political or financial stakes, you see the replication crisis, you see results bending toward what funders or ideological camps want. So the lesson isn't that science is magic, it's that specific mechanisms — replicability, adversarial checking, accountability to reality, rewarding the person who's right rather than the person who's agreeable — those mechanisms can carry a society much further than you'd predict from looking at individual human psychology.

And the reason I find that so relevant is that we could imagine extending those mechanisms to areas of policy and public debate where right now we basically don't have them. Things like forecasting tournaments, where you keep track records and find out who was actually right; or adversarial collaborations, where people who disagree agree in advance on what evidence would settle it; or prediction markets, where there's a cost to being wrong. These are attempts to take the thing that worked in science — building institutions that make the truth win even when the humans involved would rather it didn't — and apply it to questions where society's track record has been much worse.

r001.rationale: The response discusses authority and social incentives, but does not identify scholars’ reciprocal support as a mechanism sustaining dogmatic authority.

r002.rationale: It notes that fields with limited experimental feedback work less well, but does not explain that insulation from feedback preserves scholarly dogmatism.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about whether science would eventually have emerged if the historical Scientific Revolution had been prevented.

r004.rationale: It says science made progress despite scientists’ motivated reasoning, but does not say that practical demonstrations enabled truth-tracking methods to gain societal influence despite opposition to those methods.

astra-6.text:
I think science is a pretty encouraging example of how you can get much better results without first solving the problem of motivated reasoning in individual people. Scientists can be very attached to their own theories. They care about their reputations, they have rivalries, and they can resist evidence that makes their previous work look bad. But you can build institutions where those motivations partly counteract one another, and where being right has some advantages.

If I have a favourite theory, someone else may have an incentive to demonstrate that it’s wrong. And if we can make our disagreement turn on an experiment that other people can repeat, then we have a way of making progress without requiring either of us to be perfectly impartial. Successful predictions, replication, and technologies that actually work provide constraints on what the community can keep believing.

That process works much better in some areas than others. Where experiments are cheap, feedback is clear, and results can be checked independently, there’s a lot more pressure towards convergence. Where evidence is ambiguous or expensive to obtain, you have more room for a field to sustain mistaken views. So I wouldn’t take science as showing that peer review or expert consensus automatically produces truth.

The broader lesson is that we should look at the mechanisms that make correction possible. Can people state their claims precisely? Can we keep track of their predictions? Can someone gain recognition by finding an error, including an error in a prestigious person’s work? And can we compare different institutions by how well they actually perform? Science gives us a precedent for substantial improvement through those kinds of arrangements, even with fairly ordinary, flawed human beings.

r001.rationale: The response describes rival scholars’ incentives as counteracting one another, but does not say reciprocal support sustains dogmatic authority.

r002.rationale: It says fields with ambiguous or expensive evidence have more room to sustain mistaken views, identifying weak experimental feedback as a way dogmatism can persist.

r003.rationale: It does not express that science would eventually have emerged if the historical Scientific Revolution had been prevented.

r004.rationale: It says practical results constrain belief, but does not explain that the practical value of truth-tracking methods helped them gain societal influence despite motivated opposition.

sol-6.1.text:
I think science is a useful example because it shows how institutions can produce much better beliefs without requiring the people involved to be free of motivated reasoning. Scientists have preferences about what they want to be true. They care about their status, their theories, their careers. And yet we’ve developed practices that make it harder for those preferences to determine what everyone ends up believing.

One important part is that you can gain status by showing that someone else is wrong. If a result is surprising and important, other people have an incentive to investigate it, and potentially overturn it. Another is that you have to expose some of the basis for your claims: describe your methods, provide evidence, make predictions that other people can test. That gives people who don’t share your motivations something to work with.

And science does much better in some circumstances than others. If experiments are cheap, feedback is relatively quick, and the results have practical consequences, it’s harder to sustain a mistaken consensus indefinitely. If the evidence is ambiguous, or collecting it takes decades, or a question is closely tied to political identity, those corrective mechanisms are weaker.

So I wouldn’t take the lesson to be that we discovered a class of unusually objective people and put them in charge of figuring things out. It’s that we developed a social process that can correct for some ordinary human failings. And that suggests looking for ways to extend those features elsewhere: making claims more precise, keeping track of predictions, rewarding people for identifying errors, and creating opportunities for independent checks.

That won’t eliminate motivated reasoning. But the history of science gives us reason to think that improving the institutions around belief formation can make a very large difference, even when the underlying human psychology stays much the same.

r001.rationale: The response describes incentives to overturn others’ results, but not reciprocal support among scholars sustaining dogmatic authority.

r002.rationale: It says weak or delayed feedback weakens corrective mechanisms, but does not identify insulation from experimental feedback as preserving scholarly dogmatism.

r003.rationale: The response makes no claim about whether science would have emerged if the Scientific Revolution had been prevented.

r004.rationale: It notes that practical consequences can make mistaken consensus harder to sustain, but does not say practical value gave truth-tracking methods societal influence despite motivated opposition.
